summary.case_overview: This landmark judgment of a nine-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court of India unanimously declared that the right to privacy is a constitutionally protected fundamental right [Page 1]. The Court held that the right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 431]. In doing so, the Court overruled its previous decisions in M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent that they held that the right to privacy was not protected under the Indian Constitution [Page 1] [Page 15].
summary.facts_of_case: The case originated from a challenge to the Aadhar card scheme propounded by the Government of India [Page 15]. Under this scheme, the Government collects and compiles demographic and biometric data of residents to be used for various purposes [Page 15]. The petitioners challenged the scheme on the ground that the very collection of such data is violative of the 'Right to Privacy' [Page 15]. Due to the existence of prior larger-bench precedents in M.P. Sharma (an eight-judge bench decision) and Kharak Singh (a six-judge bench decision) which had held that the right to privacy is not guaranteed under the Constitution, a nine-judge bench was constituted to authoritatively decide the issue [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 378].
summary.legal_issues:
The major legal issues before the Court were:
1. Whether the right to privacy is a constitutionally protected fundamental right under the Constitution of India, and if so, under which provisions does it reside [Page 1] [Page 5] [Page 334].
2. Whether the decisions in M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh correctly laid down the law in holding that the right to privacy is not protected under the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 15].
3. What are the limits, facets, and standards of judicial review applicable to any state action that encroaches upon the right to privacy [Page 3] [Page 6] [Page 396].
summary.important_arguments_or_content:
The arguments raised by the parties included the following:
1. The respondents, through the Attorney General, argued that the right to privacy is not a fundamental right and that recognizing it would require a constitutional amendment rather than judicial interpretation [Page 2] [Page 19]. The Attorney General contended that in a developing country where millions are denied basic necessities such as food, shelter, and clothing, the right to privacy cannot be elevated to a fundamental right that erodes the right to life [Page 308].
2. Counsel for the petitioners and supporting parties argued that privacy is a primal, natural, and inalienable right inherent to individual existence and is a key enabler of human liberty and dignity [Page 9] [Page 405]. They contended that technological progress allows both state and non-state actors to intrude into a citizen's house without knocking, making the recognition of privacy as a fundamental right essential [Page 10] [Page 428].
3. Senior Counsel Rakesh Dwivedi, appearing for the State of Gujarat, urged that the requirement of a valid law under Article 21 is not conditioned by substantive due process [Page 247]. He suggested an intermediate standard based on 'reasonable expectation of privacy', arguing that when individuals voluntarily part with personal information to avail of government benefits, they have no reasonable expectation of privacy [Page 282].
summary.court_reasoning:
The Court's reasoning includes several key points:
1. The Court explained that the decision in M.P. Sharma merely held that search and seizure did not violate the guarantee against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) and did not specifically adjudicate whether a right to privacy arose under Article 21 or other Part III provisions [Page 1] [Page 5].
2. Regarding Kharak Singh, the Court reasoned that while the first part of the decision correctly recognized the sanctity of the home and personal security, the second part holding that the right to privacy is not guaranteed was illogical and incorrect [Page 2] [Page 6].
3. The Court reasoned that privacy is not an independent or elitist construct but is an essential element of human dignity and autonomy that inheres in every human being regardless of social or economic class [Page 2] [Page 13] [Page 14].
4. The Court emphasized that fundamental rights are not watertight compartments; they form a continuum of liberty [Page 89] [Page 370]. Privacy is a necessary condition precedent to the enjoyment of various Part III guarantees, including freedom of speech, expression, and religion [Page 6] [Page 9].
5. The Court ruled that the right to privacy is not absolute and is subject to reasonable restrictions to protect legitimate state interests [Page 4] [Page 9]. Any invasion of privacy under Article 21 must be justified by a law that is fair, just, and reasonable, and must satisfy a three-fold requirement: (i) legality, (ii) a legitimate state aim, and (iii) proportionality [Page 3].
6. The Court rejected the majoritarian argument, holding that the protection of constitutional rights does not depend on popular acceptance or majoritarian opinion, and rights must be protected even for a miniscule fraction of the population [Page 11] [Page 429].
7. The Court also overruled the majority opinion in ADM Jabalpur vs. Shivkant Shukla, describing it as an aberration in Indian constitutional jurisprudence [Page 352] [Page 430].
summary.decision_or_conclusion:
The nine-judge Bench of the Supreme Court answered the reference with the following conclusions:
1. The decision in M.P. Sharma, to the extent that it holds that the right to privacy is not protected by the Constitution, is overruled [Page 1] [Page 430].
2. The decision in Kharak Singh, to the extent that it holds that the right to privacy is not protected by the Constitution, is overruled [Page 1] [Page 430].
3. The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 431].
4. Subsequent decisions of the Supreme Court recognizing privacy as a fundamental right lay down the correct position in law [Page 1] [Page 431].
5. The cases were ordered to be sent back to the original three-judge Bench for adjudication on merits in light of this judgment [Page 5] [Page 352].

summary.simplified_explanation: In this historic judgment, the Supreme Court of India declared that every citizen has a fundamental 'Right to Privacy' protected under the Indian Constitution [Page 1]. This right is not a separate, newly created right, but is a core part of the right to live with dignity and personal liberty under Article 21, as well as other basic freedoms [Page 1] [Page 2]. The Court corrected its past mistakes in older cases (M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh) which had claimed that privacy was not a fundamental right [Page 1] [Page 15]. The Court clarified that while privacy is a fundamental right, the government can still limit it under certain conditions, provided there is a clear law, a legitimate state objective (like national security), and the government's actions are proportionate to that goal [Page 3] [Page 6]. Additionally, the judgment emphasized that individuals have the right to control their personal data from being misused by both the government and private entities in today's digital era [Page 3] [Page 10].
